'''Walter Gautschi''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɡ|aʊ|tʃ|i}}; {{Respell|GOW|chee}}; born December 11, 1927) is a Swiss-born American [[mathematician]], [[writer]] and [[Emeritus|professor emeritus]] of [[Computer science]] and [[Mathematics]] at [[Purdue University]] in [[West Lafayette, Indiana]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Walter Gautschi - Department of Computer Science - Purdue University |url=https://www.cs.purdue.edu/people/faculty/wxg.html |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=www.cs.purdue.edu |archive-date=2023-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230504210750/https://www.cs.purdue.edu/people/faculty/wxg.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He is primarily known for his contributions to [[numerical analysis]]<ref>[[Philip J. Davis]], [http://history.siam.org/oralhistories/gautschi.htm Walter Gautschi] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513024715/http://history.siam.org/oralhistories/gautschi.htm |date=2008-05-13 }}, interview [[Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] (December 7, 2004)</ref> and has authored over 200 papers in his area and published four books.

== Early life and education ==
Gautschi was born December 11, 1927, in [[Basel|Basel, Switzerland]], to Heinrich Gautschi (1901-1975). His paternal family originally hailed from [[Reinach, Aargau|Reinach]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eduard Gautschi (1900–1965) |url=https://kunstbreite.ch/Kuenstlerwerdegaenge_aargau_gautschi_eduard.htm |access-date=2023-12-04 |website=kunstbreite.ch |archive-date=2023-12-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231204220049/https://kunstbreite.ch/Kuenstlerwerdegaenge_aargau_gautschi_eduard.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> He had one twin brother Werner (1927-1959). He completed a [[Ph.D.]] in [[mathematics]] from the [[University of Basel]] on the thesis ''Analyse graphischer Integrationsmethoden'' advised by [[Alexander Ostrowski]] and [[Andreas Speiser]] (1953).<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=16467}}
</ref>

== Career ==
Since then, he did postdoctoral work as a Janggen-Pöhn Research Fellow at the ''Istituto Nazionale per le Applicazioni del Calcolo'' in [[Rome]] (1954) and at the [[Harvard Computation Laboratory]] (1955). He had positions at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] (1956–59), the [[American University]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], the [[Oak Ridge National Laboratory]] (1959–63) before joining [[Purdue University]] where he has worked from 1963 to 2000 and now being [[professor emeritus]]. He has been a [[Fulbright]] Scholar at the [[Technical University of Munich]] (1970) and held visiting appointments at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] (1976), [[Argonne National Laboratory]], the [[Wright-Patterson Air Force Base]],  [[ETH Zurich]] (1996-2001), the [[University of Padova]] (1997), and the [[University of Basel]] (2000).<ref>[http://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/wxg/ homepage] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080924055126/http://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/wxg/ |date=2008-09-24 }} at [[Purdue University]].</ref>

As well-known (e.g. Gerhard Wanner, Geneva {{circa|2011}} and the well-known first-hand sources and subsequent reports such as Math. Intelligencer, etc), one of Gautschi's most important contributions on numerical simulation of special functions offered evidence and confidence to [[Louis de Branges|de Branges]]'s tour-de-force attack on the elusive [[Bieberbach conjecture]] on the magnitude of coefficients of schlicht functions, which hitherto received only slow, difficult and partial progress by work of Bieberbach, Loewner, Gabaredian and Schiffer.

== Personal life ==
In 1960, Gautschi married Erika, who was previously married to his twin brother Werner (1927-1959). Werner was also an academic professor and lecturer and emigrated to the [[United States]] with his wife in 1956. After his sudden death, Erika returned to Switzerland, while being pregnant with her child to [[Basel]] where she met Walter and married him in 1960.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Obituaries in West Lafayette, IN {{!}} Journal and Courier |url=https://jconline.com/obituaries/ljc063166 |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=jconline.com |language=en}}</ref> They had three daughters;

* Theresa (1961-2018), married Ainsworth, two children; Emily Ainsworth (b. 1994) and Keith (b. 1997), formerly of [[Camas, Washington]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Theresa Gautschi-Ainsworth Obituary (2018) - Camas, Wa., IN - Journal & Courier |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/jconline/name/theresa-gautschi-ainsworth-obituary?id=12190182 |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=Legacy.com |archive-date=2023-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230504210749/https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/jconline/name/theresa-gautschi-ainsworth-obituary?id=12190182 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Doris (b. 1965)<ref>{{Cite web |title=ABOUT |url=https://www.joyful-math.com/about |access-date=2023-05-04 |website=Joyful Math |language=en |archive-date=2023-05-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230504210750/https://www.joyful-math.com/about |url-status=live }}</ref>
* Caroline ''Cari'' (b. 1969)

Through his predeceased twin brother, he has stepson/nephew, Thomas (b. 1960). Gautschi still resides in [[West Lafayette, Indiana]].

*''Numerical analysis: an introduction'', Birkhäuser, Boston, 1997;<ref>{{cite journal|author=Stetter, Hans J.|authorlink=Hans Jörg Stetter|title=Review of ''Numerical analysis, an introduction'' by Walter Gautschi|journal=Math. Comp.|year=1999|volume=68|issue=226|page=887|doi=10.1090/S0025-5718-99-01151-5|doi-access=free}}</ref> 2nd edition, 2012.
*''Orthogonal polynomials: computation and approximation'', Oxford University Press, Oxford, 2004.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Review of ''Orthogonal Polynomials: Computation and Approximation'' by Walter Gautschi|author=Segura, Javier|journal=SIAM Review|volume=48|issue=2|date=June 2006|pages=431–433|jstor=20453824}}</ref>

*''Orthogonal polynomials in [[MATLAB]]: exercises and solutions'', SIAM, Philadelphia, 2016.<ref>{{cite web|author=Townsend, Alex|title=Review of ''Orthogonal polynomials in MATLAB: exercises and solutions'' by Walter Gautschi|url=https://www.math.cornell.edu/~ajt/papers/Gautschi.pdf|website=www.math.cornell.edu/~ajt}}</ref>
